## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Susīmajātaka* (Ja 163) is a birth story preserved in the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. The commentary frames the narrative as having been delivered by the Buddha while staying at Jetavana near Sāvatthi, prompted by the practice of arbitrary almsgiving (*chandakadāna*) among the city's inhabitants [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The verse opening the tale begins *Kālamigā setadantā tava ime* ("Five score black elephants...") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879].
In the traditional resolution (*samodhāna*) that connects the story of the past to the present assembly, the Buddha identifies the principal figures of the narrative: the Bodhisatta was the young brahmin pupil (*māṇava*), his parents were King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, King Susīma was Ānanda, and the renowned master teacher (*disāpāmokkhācariya*) was Sāriputta [Fausböll 1879].
Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus reports any internal Pali text reuse or cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan for this Jātaka [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral]. SuttaCentral lists four modern translations of the text in four languages [SuttaCentral].
